1	# The library
2	
3	The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:
4	
5	- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it.
6	- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
7	- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. An edit to it needs the library order (`build-and-caches.md`).
8	- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. No running program imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.
9	
10	`Library/FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. Never edit them by hand.
11	
12	A `for` loop, a comprehension and a big operator such as `SUM` are calls into the library. The shared desugarer turns a `for` loop into a call of its generator's `loop` method. It turns a comprehension or a reduction into calls of `__generate` and `__bigOperator`. These work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.
13	
14	## The curator's decisions on the library
15	
16	Build on these decisions:
17	
18	- Exclusion (`excludes`, `comprises`) is used all over the library. The compiled checker keeps the multiple-instantiation exclusion rule.
19	- The numeric tower is flat. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR64` and `RR32` are siblings under `Number`, and each carries its own algebra. A wider type has a `coerce` from each narrower type. Walk converts by coercion at dispatch.
20	- The implicit bound of an unbounded type parameter is `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`.
21	- A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.
22	- A conversion is applied to make a call possible. It never changes which declaration runs if one already fits.
23	- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
24	- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
25	- Fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` on both paths. Code that means to wrap uses the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
26	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. If nothing at the call fixes the element type, write it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Under walk, an unwritten element type dies at the first element (ledger row 424).
27	- A `nat` static parameter is an `NN32` value, and an `int` parameter is a `ZZ32` value. A larger size is refused.
28	
29	## Designing a change
30	
31	- Put extensions into this library itself, never into a separate library tree of our own. Do not add a declaration to the compiler's prelude.
32	- Do not design a fix from a reading of the specification alone, or from a workaround on the user's side.
33	- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses how you want to write something, find how the library already writes that kind of thing. Do the same.
34	- When you add a method, choose a dotted method or a functional method as the library does in the same family. The team proposed this rule: an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`). The family's own practice comes first.
35	- One type must not declare a dotted method and a functional method of the same name. A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
36	- The name of a new functional method is reserved in every program that imports the library. A program that uses the name for a variable or a parameter is then refused: "Variable even is already declared."
37	- Before you choose, search the curator's decisions (`records.md`).
38	- If the library's practice and the specification's text disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
39	
40	## Editing
41	
42	- A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Compare parse trees or diagnostics only after you map the positions back (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/parse-compare.sh` and `remap-lines.py`).
43	- Put tests of walk's behaviour of the library in `ProjectFortress/tests/`. `library_tests/` holds compiled tests of the compiler's prelude.
44

1	# The compiled checker, the code generator and the run time
2	
3	The code of this area is in these directories:
4	
5	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
6	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
7	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
8	
9	The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.
10	
11	## Which desugarings run on each path
12	
13	Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:
14	
15	- coercion;
16	- chained comparisons;
17	- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
18	- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
19	- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.
20	
21	Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if you fix one of these desugarers, only the compiled path changes. If walk is wrong there, fix the evaluator.
22	
23	## What the two paths share
24	
25	After the phases, each path has its own code for these:
26	
27	- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
28	- Number natives: walk's `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`), and the compiled `nativeHelpers/` (`simpleIntArith.java`).
29	- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
30	- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.
31	
32	So a fix of a rule on one path is not a fix on the other. In your report, say which path you fixed, and whether the other path has the same defect.
33	
34	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
35	
36	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.
37	
38	- Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay.
39	- The record does not yet say what happens to `CompilerSystem` at the switch-over.
40	
41	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
42	
43	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
44	
45	- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
46	- a local function declaration, and an object expression;
47	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.
48	
49	It also refuses a function, object or trait declaration with a `where` clause or a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`).
50	
51	The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
52	
53	Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).
54	
55	## What the code generator does
56	
57	`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time", gives the jars, the dispatch methods, the templates and the boxed numbers.
58	
59	- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
60	- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
61	- The `value` modifier has no effect on the representation.
62	- The curator decided that array storage will be an unboxed `double[]`. This is not built yet. The other questions of the array design wait until after the switch-over. If your task touches how arrays are stored, print both decisions first (about 2 KB):
63	
64	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:Storage is' 'positions:array design'
65	
66	## The run time
67	
68	- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Open ledger rows name it, such as rows 408 and 559.
69	- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches.
70	
71	## Natives
72	
73	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
74	
75	The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method.
76	
77	## Traps of the compiled path
78	
79	- Before disambiguation, the compiled path bounds an unbounded type parameter by `Object`, not `Any`. Walk does not. So the compiled path rejects every generic that is instantiated at a tuple type, until the switch-over (ledger row 412).
80	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
81	- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. The team turned it off in 2012 (`c35aac139`). If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
82	
83	## The `fortress` commands
84	
85	`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
86	
87	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
88	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
89	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
90	- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.
91	
92	## Running
93	
94	    cd ProjectFortress
95	    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
96	    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
97	    ../bin/fortress run P [args]
98	
99	A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.
100	
101	- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
102	- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead: it gives the cause.
103	
104	## Before an edit
105	
106	Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. Both were written in September 2026, before the revival's batches, so a status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.
107	
108	- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.
109	
110	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'
111	
112	- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the run time and B.12 the natives.
113	
114	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'
115	
116	- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. 224 of the 549 `.test` files in `compiler_tests/` pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. Update each one in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.
117	
118	## Testing an edit here
119	
120	- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory. Compile it against the class path on the last line that `bin/fortress_classpath` prints. Put that directory first on the class path. This takes seconds, rebuilds nothing and changes nothing tracked.
121	- Give such a run its own caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES` under your `tmp/`), because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
122	- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).
123

1	# The interpreter (walk)
2	
3	Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:
4	
5	- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
6	- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
7	- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
8	- `glue/`: the natives.
9	
10	## How walk evaluates a program
11	
12	After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.
13	
14	At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.
15	
16	Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. This is an accepted limit until the switch-over.
17	
18	## What walk checks
19	
20	Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). No command checks them for a walk program: `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
21	
22	At load, walk checks the overload sets and some `comprises` clauses. It refuses:
23	
24	- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if their declared domains order a generic declaration and a plain one, or if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap.
25	- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`) in a type that provides both.
26	- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
27	- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses.
28	
29	So a library edit that adds an overload can stop every program at load. `tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.
30	
31	Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.
32	
33	## Natives
34	
35	The library binds each of walk's natives by a string in its `.fss` files: `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X")`. The classes are in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. They take the evaluator's boxed values, so the compiled path cannot use them. `import java`, the compiled path's way to bind natives, is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it.
36	
37	To raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees, a native throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `Int.java` there makes one, and its callers throw it:
38	
39	    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
40	    return new FortressError(f);
41	
42	A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other exception from a native ends the run, a division by zero too.
43	
44	## Running a program
45	
46	    bin/fortress P.fss
47	
48	- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
49	- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
50	- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
51	- Your setup sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, the size of the pool, to 1 (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"). If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs.
52	- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches.
53	- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.
54	- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/mandelbrot_canonical.fss`, which prints its picture, or `bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss`, which prints nothing and exits 0. Do not use `explorations/claude_demo.fss`: it dies under walk (ledger row 424). `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.
55	
56	## The model program
57	
58	MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. To check the model after a library change, run `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. It runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from an empty private cache and writes `<work-dir>/<name>.txt`. Read its `VERDICT:` line and its last line, `rc=`.
59	
60	- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.
61	- If you change a line of the model, put the change in your report as a diff.
62	
63	## After an edit here
64	
65	An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches in `Shell.java`, can change both paths. Walk turns some desugarings off: `compiler.md`, "Which desugarings run on each path", lists them. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only. `compiler.md`, "What the two paths share", says what to report then.
66

1	# Writing a test
2	
3	A test is gated if the gate's suites run it. The harness reports each test green, or red: a failure in JUnit's verdict. An `XXX` test is a gated expected failure: it asserts the answer that the specification gives, and fails today. The harness reports it green while it fails, and red when the defect is fixed. A code-generator wall is a `sayWhat` call or another thrown `CompilerError` for a construct that the code generator does not compile yet.
4	
5	## A test program
6	
7	A test program has this form:
8	
9	    component Name
10	    export Executable
11	
12	    (* declarations *)
13	
14	    run(): () = do
15	        assert(f(2), 4, "f(2)")
16	    end
17	
18	    end
19	
20	- `(*)` starts a comment to the end of the line. It cannot hold `*)`: the parser ends the comment there and refuses the program. `(* ... *)` comments nest.
21	- Under walk, `assert(x, y, msg)` checks that `x` equals `y`, for values of any type. The compiler's library declares the two-value `assert` only for `ZZ32`, `String` and `Character`; its `assert(flag, msg)` takes any `Boolean`.
22	- Do not name a variable or a parameter after a functional method of the library, such as `big`, `even`, `numerator` or `shift`. The disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses it: "Variable even is already declared."
23	- Under walk, a numeral does not bind to `NN32` or `NN64`, and a numeral with a radix point does not bind to `RR32` (ledger row 454). Write `a: NN32 = unsigned(5)`, not `a: NN32 = 5`.
24	
25	## Where a test goes, and how it passes
26	
27	Interpreter (walk): write `ProjectFortress/tests/Name.fss`, whose component is `Name`.
28	
29	- Every `.fss` file there is gated, with no `.test` file needed.
30	- It is green if it throws no exception, exits 0, and neither its standard output nor its standard error contains `fail` or `FAIL`. A longer word counts too: `failure` fails the test. Only a file whose name contains `QuickCheckTest` is exempt.
31	- An api that it imports, and a helper component, go in `ProjectFortress/test_library/`. In `tests/`, a helper would run as a test.
32	- The harness skips files whose names end in `Syntax.fss`, `DynamicSemantics.fss` or `Satisfiability.fss`, or contain `GenomeUtil`.
33	- For a refusal at load, put `Name.test` beside `tests/Name.fss`, with `load_exception_contains=<message>`. A plain test is green if walk refuses the program at load as named. A failure while the top-level variables are initialised counts as a refusal. An `XXX` test with such a `.test` file is green if the program loads and runs clean.
34	
35	Compiled: write `Name.fss` and `Name.test` in the compiled test folder that holds tests of its kind:
36	
37	- `library_tests/`: the compiler's library.
38	- `parser_tests/`: the parser.
39	- `compiler_tests/`: the rest, beside the team's numbered `CompiledN` tests.
40	- `other_compiler_tests/`: the team's compiled tests that do not fit the `CompiledN` series, by the comment in `OtherCompilerJUTest.java`. The revival has added none there.
41	
42	The `.test` files are the whole list of tests: a `.fss` that no `.test` file names never runs. A `.test` file is a Java property file. It names the commands to run and the checks on their output, as lit's RUN and CHECK lines do:
43	
44	    tests=Name                 the component(s) it drives; without it, the .test file's own name
45	    compile | link | typecheck each present command is one JUnit case; link compiles, then links
46	    run                        run the linked program in a subprocess (bin/fortress run)
47	    <command>_<stream>_<check>=text
48	                               command: compile, link or run; stream: out, err or exception;
49	                               check: contains, does_not_contain, equals, matches,
50	                               WIcontains (containment with runs of whitespace collapsed)
51	
52	A `run` fails if the program exits non-zero or a `run_*` check fails. With no `run_out` check, its output must contain `pass` or `PASS`. For example:
53	
54	    tests=EqualityRung1
55	    link
56	    run
57	    run_out_WIcontains=PASS
58	
59	## How `XXX` works
60	
61	- Under walk, an `XXX` test is `tests/XXXName.fss`, whose component is `XXXName`. With no `.test` file, it is green when it fails as a plain test would.
62	- In the compiled test folders, the `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name applies to every command that the file drives: each must fail.
63	- An unmet `run_*` check makes a run test red, whatever the prefix.
64	- The harness reports any link or compile exception of a component whose name contains `XXX` as expected, whatever the `.test` file's name. Only an unmet key of that command makes it red.
65	- An `XXX` compile test with a `compile_err_contains` key, whose program compiles, reports "Saw wrong failure", which is red.
66	- A green `XXX` test prints `Saw expected failure` or `OK Saw expected exception`. JUnit's verdict counts it as passed.
67	
68	## How a defect is recorded
69	
70	Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:
71	
72	1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
73	2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. A program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time belongs here.
74	3. It is deferred, and the specification is silent or a conflict leaves it open (`exploring.md`): a test that asserts today's behaviour, and a row in the gap ledger (`records.md`). If no program can observe the defect, write the ledger row only. Its reproducer, the row's cell that names the test, is `none`, and its notes give the command and its output.
75	
76	If your brief does not let you edit the original tree, say in your report which of the three the defect needs, and write a ledger row for it, whichever it needs. A probe that only measures and reports is an example. The change that next works there writes the test.
77	
78	## The order: the test, its failure, the fix, the pass
79	
80	1. Write the test, with a plain name. Write the essence of the defect as a clean, minimal program, not the shape in which a probe met it.
81	2. See the test fail through the harness (`harness-one.sh` or `junit.sh`, `tests-running.md`) on the base's code. Do this in a run that ends before you first build or compile your edit. Under walk, do it before you edit a library source that the test reads. If your tree already holds the fix, run the base's code through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh`, which keeps its own caches (`worktrees.md`).
82	3. Make the fix. See the test pass in your last run after your last change of code.
83	
84	The test needs no commit of its own.
85	
86	In your report, quote two to five lines of the failing run and the passing line, each with its command. In an edit of the original tree, put every check into a gated test, never into a one-off script. A probe that only measures may use its own script. Assert a value with `assert` in an interpreter test. In a compiled test, assert it with `assert` (above), or print it and check it with a `run_out_equals` key. The harness checks both, so they are part of the suite's verdict.
87	
88	Check an edit of prose in `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the tree and the curator's decisions.
89	
90	## Writing an `XXX` test
91	
92	In a compiled test folder, name the component `XXXName`, in its file `XXXName.fss` and in its `component` line.
93	
94	- For a refusal at compile time, write one `XXX` compile test.
95	- For a code-generator wall, write `XXXName.test` with `tests=XXXName`, `compile` and `compile_exception_contains=<text of the exception>`.
96	- For a program that compiles and fails at run time, write two `.test` files over the component:
97	  - `NameLink.test`, a plain name, with `tests=XXXName` and `link`. It is red if the link reports static errors, but green on an exception.
98	  - `XXXName.test`, with `tests=XXXName` and `run`, and no `link`. Its run uses the plain file's link, so run the two files in one call of `junit.sh` or `fortress junit`, the plain one first.
99	  - The program prints `REACHED` in `run()` before the part that fails. The `XXX` file checks it with `run_out_contains=REACHED`, or with `run_out_does_not_contain=REACHED` if the run dies before `run()` prints. Never use `run_out_contains=PASS`.
100	  - Example: `compiler_tests/XXXBoxDotSpellingsRungW.test` and `BoxDotSpellingsRungWLink.test`.
101	
102	Show the first `XXX` test that your change adds, and only the first, working through the harness (`harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh` or `fortress junit`), from its place in a gated test folder. A direct compile and run does not show this. Run it twice:
103	
104	1. As it is: the harness must report an expected failure.
105	2. Changed for one run so that it passes, then restored: the harness must report it red. For example, add the missing declaration to the test program, or set the expected string to what the run prints.
106	
107	## Promoting an `XXX` test
108	
109	If you fix a defect that has a gated `XXX` test, the harness reports that test red. To find such a test, search the gap ledger (`records.md`): a row's reproducer names it. Also list the `XXX` files: `git ls-files 'ProjectFortress/*XXX*'`. Then:
110	
111	1. Before you edit the code, remove the prefix: give the test a plain name by its topic. Rename each file with `git mv`, or with `mv` if the file is not committed yet, and each `XXX` name inside: the `component` line, and in a compiled test the `tests=` lines and keys.
112	2. See the plain-named test fail through the harness on the base's code.
113	3. Make the fix and see the test pass.
114	
115	A run-time pair keeps its stem, and becomes three files. For example, `compiler_tests/NatRtTask` was promoted so in `fd5cb4864`:
116	
117	- `Name.fss`, with `component Name`. The program asserts its values, then prints `PASS` last.
118	- `NameLink.test`: `tests=Name` and `link`.
119	- `Name.test`, in place of `XXXName.test`: `tests=Name`, `link`, `run` and `run_out_contains=PASS`.
120	
121	## Names, comments, citations
122	
123	- Name a test by its topic. Give it one comment line that says what it checks, with no pointer to a record.
124	- Cite the specification by file and section or entry, never by line: `opr-overview.tex, subsection "GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators"`. In the library chapters, name the entry too: `basic-integers.tex, section "Integers", opr CHOOSE`.
125	- If your change breaks a line of a test that the team wrote, respell the line and keep the value that it checks. Keep every assertion. List each line's before and after in your report.
126	- If your change touches mutable state, a field, an `atomic` block or library code that writes shared state, run its checks at one thread and at four. The same holds for the Java of tasks, transactions or the class loader. `harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh` and the suites force four threads. For one thread, run the program directly with the prefix `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` (a compiled program: `compiler.md`, "Running"), and check its exit code and output.
127

1	# Running tests
2	
3	**track**
4	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`. Each track has its own caches folder, so that the four JVMs do not overwrite each other's compiled files.
5	
6	**shard**
7	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.
8	
9	**code state**
10	: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.
11	
12	## The two suites
13	
14	`ant testFast` runs about 1,800 tests in four tracks at once, in about 9 to 11 minutes:
15	
16	- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`.
17	- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
18	- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
19	- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.
20	
21	`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 500 tests in four shards, in about 3 to 4 minutes.
22	
23	The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:
24	
25	    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
26	
27	The two suites work in the same way:
28	
29	- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, about 4 s if nothing changed, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
30	- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
31	- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts, and each JVM keeps its caches in a folder under it. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
32	- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.
33	
34	To run a suite:
35	
36	- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
37	- Read the verdict in the last line: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one.
38	- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
39	- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.
40	
41	## The switches that the harness reads
42	
43	Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.
44	
45	- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
46	- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
47	- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
48	- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
49	- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled classes: show the output of passing tests too.
50	- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.
51	
52	## Outside the gate
53	
54	- `ant testSpecData` runs the specification's extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk. Five of its examples fail today: reductions written without their element type.
55	- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
56	- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).
57	
58	## When to run a whole suite
59	
60	- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
61	- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk or of a phase that both paths share, run whole the tests that it reaches. Run them once for each code state, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
62	  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
63	  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
64	  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, grammars, desugaring) or the parser, run both.
65	- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
66	- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
67	- After a code-generator edit, run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
68	- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests. A change of tests, prose or records only needs no whole suite.
69	
70	The suites do not check these:
71	
72	- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
73	- syntax abstraction: no gated test declares a DSL grammar (`build-and-caches.md`);
74	- the linker's aliasing of apis;
75	- `fortress unparse`;
76	- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
77	- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.
78	
79	If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.
80	
81	## One test, or a few
82	
83	Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict. An `ant` target ends with `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` or `BUILD FAILED`, and exits non-zero when it failed.
84	
85	### Interpreter tests
86	
87	Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:
88	
89	    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
90	        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]
91	
92	- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
93	- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
94	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, build it first (`worktrees.md` for a new worktree).
95	- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
96	- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
97	- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
98	- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.
99	
100	To see the whole diagnostic, with its stack frames, run the program directly:
101	
102	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress tests/X.fss
103	
104	The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").
105	
106	### Compiled tests
107	
108	Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).
109	
110	The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.
111	
112	    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
113	        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1
114	
115	- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
116	- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
117	- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
118	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
119	- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
120	- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.
121	
122	To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:
123	
124	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test
125	
126	Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.
127	
128	## One unit-test class, or one track
129	
130	To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It builds first, about 4 s if nothing changed. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.
131	
132	To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target builds first, then runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:
133	
134	- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks. The compiler track takes about 9 minutes.
135	- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
136	- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
137	- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.
138

1	# The gate
2	
3	The gate takes about 25 minutes.
4	
5	A test file is a `.fss`, `.fsi` or `.test` file directly in `ProjectFortress/tests/` or in a `ProjectFortress/*_tests/` directory.
6	
7	## What it writes
8	
9	- The landed gates' tables are in `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-<N>/gate/`: `summary.txt` and the ladder's tables.
10	- The next gate compares with the newest `summary.txt` in `climb-batch-*/gate/` or `gate-baseline/`. It finds no summary in another place or form. So if your brief asks you to land a gate's tables, put them there, in the same form.
11	- `summary.txt` is tab-separated. It has one row for each suite: `track/suite`, tests, failures, errors, skipped, read from `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/`. Lines that start with `#` follow: each build's `BUILD` and `Total time` lines and the atomic runs.
12	- The shell functions `gate_summary`, `gate_compare` and `last_landed_summary` in `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` write and compare the summary.
13	
14	## When to run
15	
16	Your brief says whether you run the gate. If it does not ask, do not run it: run your own tests (`tests-running.md`).
17	
18	Run the gate once for each tree. Run it again only if the tree changed under `ProjectFortress/` (test files excepted), under `Library/`, or in `build.xml`. The commit that landed the newest gate summary has the gated tree's code: that commit adds only records and the specification's PDF. This test tells you whether to run the gate again:
19	
20	    G=$(git log -1 --format=%H -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt')
21	    git diff --quiet $G HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library build.xml || echo "changed: run the gate again, unless only test files changed"
22	
23	If only test files changed, run the changed files through `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` instead (`tests-running.md`). The gate's tables then stay valid.
24	
25	## What it runs
26	
27	Run these steps in this order, on a clean build of the tree:
28	
29	1. Check `df -h /`. Warning: deleting `/tmp/fortress*rats` can break other live runs. If less than 1 GB is free, delete `/tmp/fortress*rats`, `ProjectFortress/test-tmp` and `ProjectFortress/test-caches`, and check again. If less than 500 MB is still free, stop and report.
30	2. Run `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS`, then `ant compileAll`.
31	3. If step 2's build printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, run the library order (`build-and-caches.md`). At once, before anything else compiles into the caches, make two copies of `default_repository/caches` for the ladder regression (step 7).
32	4. Run `ant testFast` (9 to 11 min), then `ant testSystem` (3 to 4 min). Both must have zero failures.
33	5. Write the summary. Compare each suite's count with the last landed summary. If a count fell or a suite is gone, the gate is red.
34	6. Do the four-thread atomic runs (about 1 min).
35	7. Do the ladder regression (about 4 min).
36	
37	## The atomic runs
38	
39	The suites run at four threads, once each, so a rare lost update or race can pass them. These runs compile fourteen programs and run each one three times at four threads, 42 lines. Run them from `ProjectFortress/`, after the library order:
40

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go, on the branch that you work on, and push that branch (below).
4	
5	Scratch includes logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs and lists. Your tree's `tmp/` is gitignored. A private caches folder outside `tmp/` is not.
6	
7	## What to commit
8	
9	- Commit the Fortress change and its tests, your report if it is a file, and a reusable script.
10	- Commit your lines for the ledger, FACTS or the plan with your work (`records.md`, "Writing to the record").
11	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`.
12	- Do not commit a copyrighted PDF or deck. `research/decks/` is gitignored. Cite such a source by its Wayback URL. `research/extracts/` holds our own summaries, with brief attributed quotations.
13	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
14	
15	## How to commit
16	
17	- Commit as you go, each commit in one command. Never commit a directory copy, and never use `git add -A`:
18	
19	      git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
20	
21	- Other agents may have uncommitted edits in the same tree. The command above commits none of them. Leave them alone.
22	- Before you commit a staged change of more than a few hundred lines, read `git diff --cached --stat`.
23	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
24	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer the harness suggests. If the work moves to another session, `explorations/protocol.md` gives the new session line.
25	
26	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
27	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
28	
29	## Pushing
30	
31	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
32	
33	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`.
34	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
35	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
36	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, do not push. That agent pushes right after it commits, so look again shortly. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
37	  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:
38	
39	         git push origin main
40	         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
41	         git push origin main:blinded-fable
42	
43	     The third push keeps current `blinded-fable`, the branch that the coordinating session was created from. A rebuilt container clones it (the `cloud-container` skill, a lost container).
44	- Push no other branch unless your brief names it.
45

\section{Changes Made by the 2026 Revival to the Working Draft}
\seclabel{revival-changes}
\sloppy

This section lists the changes made to this working draft by the 2026
revival of the Fortress project (\url{https://github.com/palimondo/fortress}).
The revival works to finish what the designers intended, judged by this
working draft, and changes the text only where a decision it has taken for
the implementation would otherwise leave the text and the implementation in
open disagreement.
Each changed passage carries a box headed
``Revised by the 2026 revival'' that points to its entry here.

Each entry gives the affected sections, the change, its rationale, its
effect, the original text, and what reversing to the alternative not taken
would require.
The original text is that of the \emph{Working Draft of February 2011},
the unrevised copy of this document kept in the revival's repository under
the directory \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/}, cited by path and line
there.
The directory's name is misleading: its sources are the working draft of
2~February 2011, and only the file \nolinkurl{fortress.1.0.pdf} in it is the
Fortress~1.0 release.
The full reasoning behind every entry, with each original passage and each
new one, is in the revival's decision records,
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md}
and, for the number chapters,
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/decision-record.md},
in the same repository.

Each change below follows a decision of the revival.
The first of those decisions, taken on
24~September 2026 and called \emph{route~A}, is that the compiled type checker keeps
the type group's rule that no type is a subtype of two different
instantiations of one parameterized trait, a rule this working draft never
stated, and that the library's numeric types are reorganized so that they
satisfy it.
An entry whose change does not follow from route~A says so, and names the
decision it follows or gives its reason.
The revision of the number chapters (\secref{revival-numbers} to
\secref{revival-reductions}) also carries out three decisions of
26~September 2026 that follow from route~A: on the refined number types, on
conversions between number types, and on sums and products.
The alternative not taken, \emph{route~C}, is described once, in
\secref{revival-routec}.

The Fortress libraries are divided into two basic categories.  The
first, covered in \chapref{default-libraries}, are the libraries that
are automatically imported by every Fortress component and API,
chiefly \TYP{FortressLibrary} and \TYP{FortressBuiltin}.  These
libraries provide the basic numeric types, generators, arrays,
booleans, exceptions, and the like.  The second, covered in
\chapref{optional-libraries}, are libraries that must be explicitly
imported by the programmer.  These include \TYP{List}, \TYP{Set}, and
\TYP{Map}.

The documentation in \partref{library} is largely automatically

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record

POSITIONS.md:26
- **The type group's late positions outweigh the early text.** The specification "was written in a vacuum early on", "as a wish"; "then the type group went in and tried to make it run. So they knew much more about what's feasible and what's not. The goal was performance. The specialization is a must"; "when that wish met reality, then the spec must change"; "whatever the spec was dreaming about in 2008 is irrelevant because it met hard reality". So the late, implementation-informed positions of the type group (the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiled tower flattened by Steele in 2011, Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper) outweigh the specification's earlier text where they conflict, and the implementers' later word outweighs unfinished text. "We are not Naden. We know nothing here."

POSITIONS.md:25
- **The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it.** Where the Types chapter of the team's unfinished restart (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`) covers a topic, it is cited beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word: the exclusion rule as "instantiation exclusion" in its two-part form, the `covariant` modifier, `Bottom` inexpressible. "On the rule S revises, it is the designers' latest intent, and the goal is to finish what they intended."

POSITIONS.md:87
- **The S1 form**, the layered form the team used for 1.0 and its 2009 draft: a labelled callout at each changed passage that prints in every build (not a `\note`); a revival section in Appendix I (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), each entry with the reason, the original sentences quoted with their path and line in the unrevised copy, and route C with what reversing to it would take; one paragraph in the front matter; the full reasoning in a repository document. The unrevised copy is called "the Working Draft of February 2011", in the team's own form, each citation giving the path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; Appendix I says once that the directory's name is misleading, since only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Appendix I's introduction says that the entries follow the revival's decisions, route A the first of them, each naming its own.

POSITIONS.md:88
- **The refused examples (S2).** Each example the exclusion rule refuses is revised to the one library's shape, the original kept in the text as "Not allowed", the specification's own form, and the rule stated once in Luchangco's two-part form under "instantiation exclusion". Built. The `covariant` keyword gets one sentence in the revival callout at the covariance example, saying that the type group's later design declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, implemented on neither path, and pointing to the decision record and row 404. The number chapters (`basic-lib/basic-integers.tex`, `basic-lib/numbers.tex`, `advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex`) changed in the same batch as the flattening, never earlier. The calculi of Appendix A (Core Fortress with Where Clauses, ACFFD and Basic Core) each carry a `\revision` callout saying that the calculus predates instantiation exclusion and admits the shapes the rule refuses, their rules and soundness claims untouched. The judgement's candidate ledger rows 2, 3 and 5 are parked (`PLAN.md`).

POSITIONS.md:86
- **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** "our plan needs to update the spec with the change that we do and somehow properly record why we decided that way, so that there is no open discrepancy between the spec and our implementation that would be confusing to people. We need to preserve the original historic record somewhere in a document with our reasoning why we did the switch and preserve the option to go the route C." \subsection{Instantiation exclusion}
\seclabel{revival-rule}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{trait-types}; \secref{trait-decls}.
\item[Change] A property of the exclusion relation is added:
two instantiations of the same parameterized trait exclude each other
unless every static argument other than an operator argument is the same.
The rule it imposes on declarations is added beside the example of
\TYP{InclusiveMolecule}: a trait or object may not extend two such
instantiations, directly or through its supertraits.
\item[Rationale] Without the rule a value may belong to two instantiations
of one parameterized trait, and code specialised for one of them can be
chosen for a caller that was promised the other; with the rule relaxed, the
compiled implementation accepts such a program and fails at run time.
The type group adopted the rule as \emph{multiple instantiation exclusion}
(Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type
Checking Modular Multiple Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and
Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011), and the compiled type checker has
enforced it since 2010.
The team's later, unfinished Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) states it in
the two parts used here, under the name \emph{instantiation exclusion}.
The type group's paper of 2019 states it as its rule [Anc-Same-Trait], which
it credits to Steele and Chase in 2012: a class that extends two instances of
a trait extends an instance below both, which for an invariant static
parameter is the same instance (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, ``Polymorphic
Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance'', POPL 2019, Figure~4).
Operator arguments do not count: an operator argument only names the
operator a subtrait inherits (\secref{opr-ident}), neither implementation
distinguishes instantiations by it at run time, and the algebra of the
library chapters depends on types that are several instantiations of one
trait differing only in operator arguments.
\KWD{nat}, \KWD{int} and \KWD{bool} arguments count: they are values at
run time (\secref{natparams}, \secref{boolparams}).
\item[Effect] Programs in which a type is a subtype of two instantiations
of one parameterized trait that differ in any other static argument are no
longer valid. The compiled type checker refuses them where the arguments
that differ are types, or numerals given as \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}
arguments (row~402 of the revival's gap ledger). It does not yet refuse
them where those arguments are \KWD{bool} arguments, though it accepts boolean parameters written out (row~406),
or where one of them is a static parameter of the trait or object that extends both (row~414).
The interpreter does not check the rule.
The number chapters are revised to the reorganized numeric types
(\secref{revival-numbers}).
\item[Original text] The Working Draft of February 2011 states no such
property; its relations are ``the smallest ones that satisfy all the
properties given in those sections (and this one)''
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex}, lines
185--189), and the properties it gives for trait types are these (lines
212--216):
\begin{quote}
A trait declaration may also include an \KWD{excludes} clause,
in which case the defined trait type
excludes every type that appears in that clause.
Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type,
and the special types \TYP{()} and \TYP{BottomType}.
\end{quote}
Its rule on declarations is only that of exclusive traits,
``no trait can extend them both''
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, lines 218--222).
\item[Route C] Replaces this rule by the rule of \secref{revival-routec}.
\end{description}

## 4. The specification itself

Searching the LaTeX for the word "rationale" finds exactly one passage, and it is about component upgrade, not about the language: `Specification/basic/components/basic.tex:372`.

The rationale the spec does carry is in four other forms.

`Specification/preliminaries/intro/philosophy.tex:12-40` is the design-goals statement: a growable language, "secure Fortran", the list of languages Fortress borrowed from; `Specification/preliminaries/intro/nutshell.tex:88-95` is the one place the spec explicitly motivates a design decision ("These design decisions are motivated in part by our goal of making the scientist/programmer's life as easy as possible…").

The 230 `\note{}` boxes are the implementers' margin: they are draft-only, and they range from status ("not yet supported") to open argument. Distribution by file, highest first: `basic/lexical-structure.tex` 19, `basic/traits.tex` 15, `basic/types-vals-vars.tex` 14, `basic/memory-model.tex` 9, `basic/expressions/literals.tex` 9, `basic/declarations.tex` 9, `basic/components/source-code.tex` 9, `basic/functions.tex` 7, `basic/components/intro.tex` 7, `basic/objects.tex` 6, `advanced/parallelism-locality/defining-generators.tex` 6, `preliminaries/overview.tex` 5, `basic/tests.tex` 5, `basic/dimensions.tex` 5, then 4 or fewer in `basic/matrix-unpasting.tex`, `basic/expressions/typecase.tex`, `basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex`, `basic/conversions-coercions.tex`, `basic/trait-parameters.tex`, `basic/overloading.tex`, `basic/operators/opr-fixity.tex`, `basic/evaluation/values.tex`, `basic/evaluation/reduction.tex`, `appendices/ascii-to-unicode.tex`, `advanced/parallelism-locality/shared-local.tex`, `advanced/overloading.tex`, and others.

The substantive ones, as samples: `basic/memory-model.tex:439-441` ("The following is controversial. I think this is effectively the condition the X10 guys are trying to capture formally…") and `:376-379` ("The following doesn't fully address Bill Pugh's concerns…"); `basic/dimensions.tex:244-254`, Guy's explanation that unit information is static and is omitted from the run-time representation exactly when type information is; `basic/conversions-coercions.tex:19-37`, an open-questions list for coercion including tests, tuple and arrow types; `basic/traits.tex:174-182` and `:195-197`, Victor's observation that a trait can explicitly extend itself through hidden type variables.

`Specification/appendices/internal-document.tex` is the spec's own rationale appendix, included only in draft builds, and it inputs two files: `appendices/FAQ.tex` (235 lines of answered design questions — why multiple dispatch rather than single, `:59`; why spawn counts as IO, `:51`; core versus standard library, `:121`; why not single inheritance between objects, `:136`; juxtaposition as the only non-ALLCAPS operator name, `:90`) and `appendices/future.tex` (756 lines of proposed features organised as Syntax and Evaluation, Types, Traits and Objects, Functions and Overloading, Expressions, Operators and Coercions, Exceptions, Components and APIs, Others, Tools — largely a digest of meetings and emails, with the participants named and their positions recorded, e.g. the array/tensor discussion at `:63-76`).

The formal apparatus is the fourth form: `Specification/appendices/calculi/` holds four core calculi (basic, `where`, overloading, acffd — `appendices/calculi/calculi.tex:18-21`), and `appendices/overloading-function.tex:12` and `appendices/overloading-coercion.tex:12` are the proofs that the overloading rules admit no ambiguous or undefined call, and that coercion resolution is well defined.

`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/FAQ.tex` and `future.tex` are byte-identical to the draft's (diff), so the frozen tree adds nothing here; what differs is that the release build hides them.

`Documentation/Specification/` is a second, later, partial spec source tree in Fortify `.tick` form (build instructions at `Documentation/Specification/Prose/README.txt:12-24`, directory roles at `Documentation/Specification/README.txt:13-25`), carrying 35 `\note{}` passages of its own; its committed render `Documentation/Specification/fortress.pdf` is 65 pages, built 2012-05-31, against the draft tree's 599.

# RR32 a sibling of RR64 in the specification: the decision record

Climb batch 6.5b, rung V (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-6.5.md`, section 3, V). This record gives the full reasoning of the rung's Appendix I entry "The single-precision floating-point type" (`\secref{revival-rr32}`, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1714-1790`), of the callout it points from (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:50-56`), and of the sentence of batch 6's entry "The number types" it revises (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:485-487`). Line numbers are on this rung's tree unless they say the base (`382b9fe7f`) or the Working Draft of February 2011 (`Specification-1.0-frozen/`).

## 1. Why the specification changes

The number chapters describe the one library (POSITIONS 2026-09-26, answer 6; the number chapters under S2), and Pavol's requirement of 2026-09-24 is that no open discrepancy stand between the specification and the implementation (POSITIONS 2026-09-24, a requirement on the plan). Until this rung the library declared `value object RR32 extends RR64` (base `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:47`, `.fss:203`) with `RR64 comprises { Float, FloatLiteral, RR32 }` (base `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:291-294`), and batch 6's entry said so ("The library's ℝ32 stays below ℝ64, as before", base `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:485-486`), as a reading of batch 6's record and not a decision (`explorations/reviews/batch-6-conformance.md`, finding 3). The rung makes `RR32` a sibling under `Number` in the library; the chapter then names it, in the S1 form (POSITIONS 2026-09-26, S1): the passage edited in place, a `\revision` callout, an Appendix I entry quoting what the text said before, and this record.

## 2. What settles it

- The specification: "These types are mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them" (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:536`; the Working Draft of February 2011, `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:502`). A value of a type below `RR64` is a value of both.
- The team's later Types chapter keeps the sentence (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick:977-978`; POSITIONS 2026-09-26, the lineage note).
- Route A (POSITIONS 2026-09-24): the number types siblings under `Number`, each carrying its own algebra.
- Answer 8 (POSITIONS 2026-09-26): an exact conversion is a coercion, a lossy one explicit. Every `RR32` value is exact in `RR64` (a binary32 value is a binary64 value), so `RR64` coerces from `RR32`, and the conversion the other way (`narrow`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:379-380`) stays explicit.
- The coercion chapter's worked example declares `trait ℝ32` and `trait ℝ64` apart, `ℝ64` with `coerce(x: ℝ32) widens`, and computes `c + a·b` with `a`, `b : ℝ32` and `c : ℝ64` by `ℝ64`'s `+` after coercing the `ℝ32` product (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:875-927`, the Working Draft's `:844-896`).
- The team's built intent: the compiler library has `RR32` and `RR64` siblings, `trait RR32 extends { Number, Equality[\RR32\] } excludes { ZZ64, ZZ32, RR64 }` and `RR64`'s `coerce(x: RR32)` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:475`, `:433-435`). They have been siblings there since Chase's `6896886fb` of 2009-08-31, whose message says "RR32 is NOT a subtype of RR64" and ends "this would be a good time to get coercion working"; that change added no coercion. `coerce(x: RR32)` is first seen in `26718e298` (2011-12-06),
....
## 5. What reversing would take

Restoring `value object RR32 extends RR64`, `RR64`'s `comprises` of `RR32` and the `b:RR64` parameters of `RR32`'s natives, and this text; row 435's defect returns with it (`ProjectFortress/tests/RR32MixedRungF.fss` would fail), and the specification's sentence of mutual exclusion would again be contradicted by the library.

\subsection{The interpreter's choice of a coercion}
\seclabel{revival-coercion-walk}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{resolving-coercion}.
\item[Change] One box after the example of the paragraph that says that
coercion is resolved statically; the paragraph and its example are unchanged.
The box says that the compiled path follows the text; that the interpreter,
which has no static types, chooses a coercion on the value and so runs
\EXP{f(B)} for the example's \EXP{f(c)}, and answers the same way wherever an
argument's value is of a type that another declaration already fits; that both
cases are gated as expected failures; and that the interpreter is to follow the
text once it takes the coercions that the compiled type checker inserts.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 29~September 2026 that the interpreter's choice of a coercion on the value is
its limit, since it has no static types from which to resolve a coercion
statically, and that the interpreter is made to follow the text once the
compiled type checker checks the programs it runs and it takes the coercions the
checker inserts.
The type group's paper of 2019 also carries the static types of calls to run
time for its dispatcher, which the interpreter does not have.
\item[Effect] None on the language.

the revival's gap ledger).

567--604, which begin:

Notice that coercion is resolved statically.  Once a coercion is statically

# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

# The specification

Three folders hold the team's specification:

- `Specification/` is the standard: the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. The text calls it "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.

Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.

A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.

The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing is the library itself, not a standard for it: cite the `.fsi` file.

## Weighing the sources

The type group is the members of the team who built the type checker and the compiler, from 2010 to 2012. Where their late positions disagree with the specification's earlier text, the curator gives the late positions more weight. These positions are:

- the exclusion rule;
- compiled code specialised to each instantiation of a generic, which they kept;
- the compiled number tower, which they flattened in 2011;
- the 2012 write-up on the Return Type Rule (`Papers/Types/journal/`);
- the POPL 2019 paper on symmetric multiple dispatch (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`).

When you describe the sources of a decision not taken (`exploring.md`), say which of them is one of these positions.

If you explore a conflict or write a decision not taken, and you need the designers' reason for a rule, print the row of its design area. WORD is a word of the area, such as `coercion`, `juxtaposition`, `dispatch` or `Arrays`. A word can match several rows, each about 1 to 2 KB.

    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:design-intent-sources.md#The map, by design area@WORD'

Then open the sources that the row names. Among them are the papers, the `\note{}` boxes, and the team's written rationale in the Internal Document appendix: `Specification/appendices/FAQ.tex` and `future.tex`.

## Changing the text: the revision form

Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.

1. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`. `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the change's Appendix I entry.

       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}

2. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect;
   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.

   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
4. The full reasoning, in a decision record under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.

If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims, and add a callout that says what the calculus predates.

## When the text and an implementation disagree

- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, change the other side to agree.
- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the conflict's ledger row in the entry's effect, beside the other departures from the text that it lists. Then the text claims no more than holds.

## Citing it

- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.
